items.title: DSA kya hai aur interview mein kaise use hota hai
items.one_idea: DSA is two things, a data structure (how data is organised) and an algorithm (the steps that use it), and an interview checks whether your steps still work when the data is huge: 10 lakh sorted names take up to 1,000,000 checks one by one but about 20 with halving.
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ने पूछा: 10 लाख names में एक name, 20 steps में कैसे ढूँढोगे?
items.hook_source: carried-over LearnAI hypothesis, first DSA test; hookscore 46.5 WEAK, no DEALBREAKER
items.visual_idea: A long row of name tiles with a magnifier moving one tile at a time and a step counter climbing toward 1,000,000, crossed out in red; then the same row halved again and again, the counter stopping at 20; chips DATA STRUCTURE (the row) and ALGORITHM (the halving moves) land on the objects when named.
items.everyday_anchor: Finding one contact among 10 lakh saved numbers: sorted list opened in the middle like a dictionary.
items.example: EXAMPLE (researcher ran it): 10 lakh sorted ints, target last: one-by-one 1000000 comparisons (worst case), halving 20. Printed: 1000000 20 True. Counts, not seconds.

items.title: Big-O: steps ka growth, seconds nahi
items.one_idea: Big-O says how the number of steps grows when the input grows: one-by-one search grows in step with the data (10 lakh to 20 lakh names is 10 lakh to 20 lakh steps), halving adds one step, checking every pair quadruples when data doubles.

items.title: Space complexity: memory dekar time bachana
items.one_idea: Space complexity says how much extra memory an algorithm needs as the input grows, and the time-space trade-off is paying memory to save steps: finding a duplicate among 10 lakh numbers takes about 5 hundred billion pair checks with no extra memory, but 10 lakh steps if you spend memory on a set.
items.spoken_hook: Code अटक रहा था, memory बढ़ाते ही चल गया।
items.visual_idea: Two lanes: pair lines vs a set shelf; step and memory bars swap sizes.
items.everyday_anchor: A shopkeeper who keeps a price list on the wall instead of recalculating every price at the counter.
items.example: EXAMPLE (ran it, Python 3.12, counts not seconds): n(n-1)/2 = 499999500000 pair checks for 10 lakh ints (n=1000: 499500; n=2000: 1999000); set: 1000000 steps; getsizeof list 8000056 B vs set 33554648 B = about 4x (container only).
facts_to_verify: Do not claim set lookup is O(1) as a Python fact.
Show real printed counts; no exact bytes or seconds on screen.
Say the set costs O(n) to build and O(n) memory.

items.title: Arrays: memory mein kaise rakhe jaate hain
items.one_idea: An array keeps its elements in one unbroken block of memory, each the same size, so the computer finds element i with one calculation (start + i x size), which makes reading any element one step, while inserting in the middle must shift every element after it (about 5 lakh moves in a 10 lakh array).
items.spoken_hook: Array में दस लाखवाँ element, एक step में कैसे?
items.hook_source: direct_question is the one of the five types not yet tested; hookscore 30.0 WEAK (Hinglish), no DEALBREAKER.
items.visual_idea: A long row of equal memory boxes with offsets 0, 4, 8 ... and a pointer jumping straight to box 999,999 by one multiplication while a crawling magnifier is crossed out; then a new value inserted in the middle makes the boxes after it slide right with a move counter reaching 5,00,000.
items.everyday_anchor: Cinema hall seats numbered in order: seat 40 is found by counting, not searching; squeezing one person into the middle moves everyone after them.
items.example: EXAMPLE (strategist ran it, researcher re-ran it 2026-10-22, Python 3.12, counts not seconds): array('i') of 1000000 ints: itemsize 4 bytes; byte offset of index 0 is 0, 1 is 4, 2 is 8, 999999 is 3999996; inserting in the middle of 1000000 items shifts 500000, of 2000000 shifts 1000000. 4 bytes is this machine's itemsize; say 'for example 4 bytes'.
facts_to_verify: Confirmed by researcher 2026-10-22. Do not claim Python list internals, real addresses, or seconds. Say 'inserting makes the elements after it move'.

items.caption_note: Day 4/150 caption. Check answer: in a 20 lakh array, inserting in the middle moves 10 lakh elements; reading index 15 lakh is still 1 step.

items.title: Strings: array jaisi, par badal nahi sakte
items.one_idea: A string is a row of characters you read by index from 0 like an array, but in Python it is immutable, so building a long string with + in a loop copies the growing string every time (model: 1000 appends copy 500500 characters) while one join copies each character once.
items.spoken_hook: String का सिर्फ़ एक letter बदलने गए, और Python ने error दे दिया। आख़िर क्यों?
items.visual_idea: letter boxes with index, blocked assignment, new row beside old, staircase of copies vs one join row.
items.everyday_anchor: A typo on a printed wedding card cannot be fixed on the card; you have to reprint a whole new card.
items.example: EXAMPLE: s='hello'; s[0]='j' raises TypeError; 1000 appends model 500500 vs join 1000; 1000000 -> 500000500000.
facts_to_verify: Python only; copy counts are a labelled model.
items.cover_headline: Why you cannot change a string

items.title: Hash map: lookup O(1) kaise ho jaata hai
items.one_idea: A hash map runs the key through a hash function to get a slot number and jumps straight to that slot, so on average a lookup does not scan the items (average O(1), not a guarantee), while a list must compare one by one.
items.spoken_hook: दस लाख में एक नाम, सीधे कैसे मिलता है?
items.hook_source: untested formula; payoff in the first line, plain words, no term used before it is explained (learnings 2026-10-22). Run hookscore on the Roman form.
items.hook_10s: दस लाख में एक नाम, सीधे कैसे मिलता है? मान लो एक list में दस लाख नाम हैं, और आखिरी नाम चाहिए, तो एक-एक करके दस लाख बार देखना पड़ेगा। Hash map में वही नाम सीधे उसकी जगह पर मिलता है। [frame 0: a long row of tiny name tiles with one arrow jumping straight to a single tile]

hook_candidates.hook: दस लाख नामों में एक नाम, सीधे मिल जाता है।
Dictionary में दस लाख में से एक key इतनी जल्दी कैसे मिलती है?
Interviewer ने पूछा: hash map में lookup तेज़ क्यों होता है?

items.visual_idea: A row of 8 numbered slot boxes. A key tile goes through a small hash box, comes out as a slot number and drops straight into that slot, with a counter showing 1 jump; beside it a list row where a pointer walks tile by tile with a counter climbing to 1000000. Then two keys landing in the same slot (EXAMPLE key mod 8) shown as a small clash, marked as the reason it is average, not always.
items.everyday_anchor: A school or office locker room: the locker number is worked out from your roll number, so you walk straight to your locker instead of opening every locker to find your bag.
items.example: EXAMPLE (labelled): 10 lakh names in a list, last name needs 1000000 comparisons (run), dict needs one lookup (run). Toy hash: key mod 8, so 10 and 18 both go to slot 2, 3 and 27 both go to slot 3 (invented, not Python's real hash). Word count with a dict and a list used as key raising TypeError unhashable were run.
facts_to_verify: Say average O(1), never worst case O(1); worst case can be O(n) with many collisions (Wikipedia Hash table).
Python dict is a resizable hash table; O(1) retrieval assumes distinct hash codes (Python design FAQ).
Keys must be hashable; a list as key raises TypeError unhashable (run it, show real output).
Run the 10 lakh list scan vs dict lookup and show the real counts; no fixed timings.
Toy mod 8 hash is labelled EXAMPLE, not how Python hashes.
Kept out as unverified: Python dict worst-case number, resize and load-factor thresholds. Optional: fetch https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/time-complexity.html for the dict row.
